AAPW: Built around one stock, Apple, using swaps to deliver about 120 percent of its weekly move while paying income out every week. With leverage that resets weekly and a single company driving everything, it is meant for short-term trading rather than long-term holding.
AJAN: Options giving exposure to the S&P 500 over a fixed two year window ending in January 2028, built to shield the value from market losses over that span. The trade-off is a cap on gains, and it only works as designed if held for the whole period.
ARKY: It builds income by mimicking autocallable notes, a kind of structured bet on individual stocks that pays regular income unless the stocks fall hard. This is a complex, engineered product: returns come from selling downside risk, so losses can arrive suddenly in a sell-off.
AUGZ: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to soften part of a market drop over an outcome period that resets each August, while giving up some gains in strong rallies. What you get depends heavily on when during the period you buy, so timing matters more here.
BBC: Small biotech companies whose main drug is still in clinical trials, spread widely so no single company dominates. It is a speculation on trial results: a successful drug can send a stock soaring, while failed trials can wipe out much of its value.
BDGS: A tactical blend of large US stocks and broad index funds, adjusted by the manager as conditions change, sometimes holding big defensive positions. With only a handful of holdings at a time, its results hinge on the manager's calls about when to be bold or cautious.
CCSO: US-listed companies selling solutions to climate change, led by industrial firms like waste handlers and building efficiency makers, plus metal producers. It is an actively managed way to back the clean transition, so it skips most of the market and swings with green industries.
CNQQ: China's biggest technology companies, from internet platforms and phone makers to battery and chip firms, chosen from the largest listed names. It is a focused bet on China's tech sector, so it swings with Chinese markets and with government policy there.
COIW: Built around one stock, Coinbase, using swaps to deliver about 120 percent of its weekly move while paying out income every week. The leverage resets weekly and everything rides on a single crypto-linked stock, so it is a short-term trading tool, not a steady holding.
CPRJ: Options on a small company stock fund, arranged to protect against losses over an outcome period that resets each July, with gains capped in exchange. It targets small company exposure with a safety net, so it should fall less than small stocks in a downturn.
CTAG: Small and mid-sized US companies picked actively for growth, led by technology, industrial and health care firms. Smaller growers like these can rise fast, but they also fall harder than big companies when investors turn cautious about risk.
CVAR: An actively managed mix of US stocks the manager judges undervalued, spread across industries with health care, technology and everyday consumer goods the largest slices. It holds only a few dozen names, so each pick matters more than in a broad index fund.
CVRT: Convertible securities, the hybrid bonds that can turn into stock, chosen for the ones most sensitive to share price moves, plus related preferred shares. It aims to join in much of a stock rally while the bond side softens falls, a middle path between stocks and bonds.
DAK: Large US stocks chosen actively, mostly held directly but partly through big index funds, with technology the largest slice. It blends stock picking with ready-made market exposure, so its results depend on the managers' picks beating a plain index fund.
DFVE: America's 500 largest companies, but each one counts the same, so smaller members matter as much as the giants. That equal weighting makes technology a much smaller slice than in the usual market-weighted funds, giving a more balanced core holding.
EART: Miners and producers of rare earths and other critical materials used in batteries, solar panels, wind turbines and electric motors, drawn from around the world. It is a focused bet on the raw ingredients of clean technology, and metal prices make it swing sharply.
EWUS: Small companies listed in the United Kingdom, spread across financial, industrial and consumer businesses. It offers a way into Britain's smaller firms, which move with the UK economy and the pound, and swing more than the country's big global companies.
FCLO: Bundles of corporate loans packaged into securities called CLOs, picked actively, spanning safer top layers and riskier lower ones. It aims for higher income than ordinary bonds, with the trade-off of credit risk if the borrowing companies run into trouble.
FDFF: Companies reshaping how money is handled: digital banks, payment networks and new-style asset managers, mostly in finance with some technology firms. It is a bet that these disruptors keep taking business from traditional banks, so it is more volatile than a plain bank fund.
FDRS: Fifty large US companies still run by the person who founded them, over half in technology, with social media, chips and car makers prominent. It bets that founders in charge keep their edge, so it concentrates in famous growth names and swings with them.
FLOW: One hundred large and mid-sized US companies chosen for generating lots of free cash flow relative to their share price, led by technology, consumer and health care firms. It tilts toward cash-rich businesses, a value style that often holds up better when growth stocks stall.
FLQS: Small US companies spread across many industries, with technology, consumer brands, health care and financials the biggest slices. It picks stocks using several measures at once, like value, quality and momentum, aiming for growth from smaller firms, which tend to swing more than big ones.
FMET: Companies building the metaverse, from chip makers and big platforms to the data centers that host virtual worlds, gathered from around the globe. It is a theme bet on virtual worlds taking off, so it moves with tech sentiment more than with actual metaverse profits.
GCAD: Makers of aircraft, aircraft parts and defense equipment, from big prime contractors to smaller specialist suppliers. It is a focused bet on aviation and military spending, actively picked in Gabelli's value style, so it moves with defense budgets and air travel demand.
GIEQ: Large and mid-sized companies from developed markets outside the US, spread across countries, with banks and industrial firms the biggest slices. Stock picking is driven by data models rather than a plain index, aiming for a core international holding with a quantitative tilt.
GLIX: Owners of essential infrastructure around the world: power and water utilities are about half, with railways, toll roads and airports making up most of the rest. It aims for steady income and steadier growth, since these businesses keep earning through good times and bad.
GSIB: The world's biggest banks, the ones regulators call systemically important because the whole financial system depends on them, spread across many countries. It is a focused bet on global banking giants, so it rises and falls with bank profits and financial stability worries.
GVLE: Large US companies the managers judge cheap relative to their worth, spread across banks, health care, technology and consumer firms. It is actively run value hunting in big stocks, so it will not mirror the index and can lag when pricey growth stocks lead.
JHMU: Municipal bonds from cities, states and public agencies across the US, actively chosen across maturities and mostly investment grade. The interest is exempt from federal income tax, and the manager can reach for extra yield with a minority of lower-rated bonds.
JNEU: Options on the S&P 500 set up to absorb the first part of a market loss over a one-year period that starts each June, with a 15% buffer as the name says. Gains above a small spread are uncapped, unlike most buffer funds that limit the upside.
KNO: Companies picked from across the developed world for how much they invest in innovation and know-how, spread over industrial, technology and health care firms. It is an actively run stock-picking fund, so its country and industry mix shifts with where the manager finds ideas.
KNOV: Options on a small company index fund, set up to absorb part of any loss over a year-long outcome period that resets each November. In return, gains are capped, and it holds options rather than the small stocks themselves, so it behaves differently from owning them.
LRNZ: Companies building artificial intelligence and deep learning tools, mostly software, cybersecurity and data firms, plus some health technology names. It is an actively managed, focused bet on AI, so its smaller technology stocks can swing sharply with the sector.
MAYU: Options on the S&P 500 set up so the fund absorbs the first part of a market drop over its one year period, which runs from May. In exchange, gains on the way up are unlimited past a small starting gap, unlike capped buffer funds.
MEDI: Health care companies of all sizes, from giant drug makers and biotech firms to device makers and drug distributors, picked actively. It is a focused bet on medicine and treatment spending, and a few large positions mean single company news can move it noticeably.
NSI: Emerging market stocks screened to leave out companies the sponsor sees as a threat to US national security. What remains leans heavily toward Asian chip makers and banks, so it still swings like an emerging markets fund, just with a security filter.
OCTZ: Options on the S&P 500 designed to absorb part of a market decline over an outcome period that restarts each October, in exchange for capped participation in big rallies. It suits investors who want a measure of protection, but results vary with when shares are bought.
OVM: Investment grade and some lower-rated municipal bonds, held through another bond fund, with an options overlay that sells put options to add income. The bond interest is tax-free at the federal level, but the option selling adds extra ups and downs on top.
PSCJ: Options on the S&P 500 arranged conservatively to keep most of the money safe while taking a modest part in market gains, over a period resetting each July. It aims for a smoother ride than stocks, accepting smaller gains in strong years in exchange for protection.
QQWZ: Large Nasdaq-listed companies, with the mix rotating by rule between the growth-heavy Nasdaq 100 lineup and a version tilted to firms with strong free cash flow. The switching rule is the point: it tries to favor whichever style is in favor at the time.
RIFR: Infrastructure owners worldwide: utilities are the biggest slice at over two fifths, with railways, toll roads, airports and energy pipelines behind them. It is built for steady income and growth from assets everyone needs, across many countries rather than just the US.
SDMF: It copies a managed futures strategy that follows price trends across markets like currencies, commodities, bonds and stock indexes, using futures contracts. Such strategies aim to make money in long up or down moves and to zig when stocks zag, adding a diversifier.
SEMI: Chip makers and the companies that supply them, plus other large technology names, with semiconductors at the center. It is a concentrated bet on the chip industry, so it rises and falls harder than the broader tech sector when chip demand shifts.
SFYF: The 50 stocks most widely held by everyday investors in SoFi brokerage accounts, led by big technology and consumer names. Because it follows what retail investors actually own, it leans heavily into popular growth stocks and can change character as fashions shift.
TAXM: An investment grade bond fund managed with taxes in mind for Massachusetts residents, mixing municipal bonds with taxable ones and aiming to keep more of the interest after tax. It is a narrow state-focused holding: the tax tailoring only pays off for Massachusetts taxpayers in higher brackets.
TEK: Technology companies from around the world, from giant chip and software makers to smaller growers, picked actively for fast, lasting growth. It goes beyond US tech, so it holds Asian chip giants too, and it swings with the global tech cycle.
THMR: A tactical mix that shifts between stocks, bonds, gold, commodities and even crypto, using other funds and some individual shares. Its managers move money toward whatever looks safer or stronger, so it can sit partly in cash when markets look risky.
TSCM: Mid-sized companies picked actively for quality growth, meaning strong businesses that can keep expanding, led by software and industrial firms. Mid-caps sit between small and large stocks, so this aims for faster growth than giants with less drama than small caps.
WARP: Companies in the space business: rocket launchers, satellite builders and operators, and the services around them. It is a narrow bet on a young industry where a few firms take most of the weight, so expect sharp swings as launches and contracts make news.
XJUL: Options on the S&P 500 that boost participation in moderate market gains up to a limit, while buffering part of a loss, over a year that resets each July. The enhanced upside is the twist on a standard buffer fund, paid for by the cap on bigger rallies.
